extracted.intended_audience: literature scholars, poets, students, and general readers interested in theories of comedy/humor
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective blog-piece that surveys major philosophical/theoretical accounts of comedy (incongruity, relief, superiority), gives examples, and proposes a Jung-inspired amendment (a doubled-consciousness or 'well, fuck me, then' effect). Useful for readers analyzing or teaching humor in literature/culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from strange, unexpected juxtaposition — the abrupt collision of incompatible elements that the understanding cannot reconcile (Kant: 'everything that is to excite a lively laugh there must be something absurd (in which the understanding, therefore, can find no satisfaction)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Monty Python philosophers playing soccer (high-culture figures in a low/pop context). Notes: the author observes that some incongruities (e.g., high/low juxtaposition) may have lost power under postmodernity, so audience familiarity and historical context affect effectiveness. Use of absurd, inexplicable juxtapositions that defeat easy explanation is central; beware that repeated or culturally flattened incongruities may not register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bakhtin's transcoding (a subtype of incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific form of incongruity that juxtaposes the high/sacred with the low/profane, often involving bodily functions (Bakhtin's notion of 'transcoding').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: carnival laughter, grotesque bodily humor. Use when deliberately mixing register (sacred/high culture) with profane/low elements to produce comic effect. Guideline: this works by shocking normative hierarchies; consider cultural taboos and audience sensibilities when deploying bodily-profanity juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory (Freud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor provides relief by violating social taboos and allowing the expression of the unsayable; laughter releases psychic pressure produced by tabooed thoughts/feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lenny Bruce-style profanity, jokes invoking forbidden stereotypes. Warning: taboo-shattering humor can 'go badly, badly wrong' — e.g., Michael Richards' career-ending n-word incident. Use with care: consider ethical implications, likely audience reaction, and risk of harm; context and performer/audience relationship are crucial. The author refrains from giving some favorite taboo examples precisely because of their offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (Thomas Hobbes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy and laughter stem from a 'sudden glory' or feeling of eminency when we sense ourselves superior to the infirmity or misfortune of others ('some sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmity of others').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: observing someone unexpectedly drenched in a fountain and feeling superior in dryness and prudence; the laughing student at Millennium Park. Use to analyze humor that depends on schadenfreude or comparative derision. Consider dynamics of observer vs. observed; the author also notes that superiority can be fleeting and situational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbesian extension: superiority to one's former self
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes allows that 'sudden eminency' can be felt relative to one's former self — e.g., narrowly avoiding a fall and laughing at the sudden improvement in one's position compared to moments earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sliding down a muddy hill but managing to stay upright and feeling superior to your previous, precarious self. Use when analyzing humor tied to sudden relief from personal peril or embarrassment; emphasizes temporal comparison rather than interpersonal comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jungian doubled-consciousness / 'well, fuck me, then' effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to Hobbesian superiority: humor arises when one experiences a doubled-consciousness — simultaneously feeling the affect (humiliation, annoyance) and observing it from a higher detached perspective, permitting laughter at oneself in the present moment ('well, fuck me, then').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the post: wife whose hat is blown off by a train, blinds unrolling and falling apart, or being shat upon by a seagull — the person both suffers and, via detachment, perceives and laughs at the suffering. Guideline: this effect accounts for laughter that is not superiority over others or past selves but a self-observational superiority while still undergoing the event. The author argues this doubled-consciousness can be cultivated as a useful skill for resilience and comic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/audience-risk guideline for taboo or transgressive comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Transgressive/taboo humor can produce catharsis or liberation for some audiences but also provoke severe backlash, offense, or career damage when misjudged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Michael Richards' n-word incident (career-ending), controversy around Tommy Tiernan's Holocaust remarks. Guidance: weigh context, performer identity, audience expectations, and potential harm. When using relief/taboo strategies, anticipate possible negative outcomes and adjust material or delivery accordingly; context and historical/cultural framing matter for interpretation.
